architectural_implications.after: A coordinator agent routing to narrow sub-agents (Figma, Gmail, Kayak, Navan, Salesforce, Google Workspace, Asset Generation).
architectural_implications.before: One general-purpose agent accumulating MCP servers and skills in a shared context window.
architectural_implications.consequence: Context per agent shrinks; permissions and capability limits become enforceable per sub-agent; tool registries must be scoped rather than global.
architectural_implications.observation: The unit of capability becomes the sub-agent boundary rather than the tool/skill slot on a single agent.

architectural_implications.after: Deterministic orchestration code (loop control, guardrails, hooks, rules) wraps non-deterministic model calls.
architectural_implications.before: The model is treated as the application, with orchestration implicit in prompts.
architectural_implications.consequence: Portability, telemetry, and durable execution become harness concerns with their own design surface, and provider abstraction can live below the agent.
architectural_implications.observation: The model, harness, and agent are separated as distinct artifacts.

architectural_implications.after: Sub-agents callable as tools, enabling recursion under a coordinator.
architectural_implications.before: Tools are external functions; agents are top-level constructs.
architectural_implications.consequence: Uniform call interface simplifies orchestration but raises questions about depth limits, cost accounting, and failure propagation across nested agents.
architectural_implications.observation: Sub-agents are represented as a tool type in the stack, alongside functions and prompts.

article_ideas.angle: Invert the standard cost-model assumption and show where the token budget actually goes per task, with the 29%–76% per-task cost increase as the counterexample to 'prices are dropping'.
article_ideas.audience: AI platform engineers, engineering managers owning agent budgets
article_ideas.based_on: token count required per task is increasing rapidly due to context bloat
article_ideas.thesis: Falling per-token prices are a distraction from the real cost lever: per-task context consumption is inflating faster than unit prices are falling, so agent cost work must target consumption — tool schemas, skill documentation, and history — not model selection.
article_ideas.title: Cheaper Tokens, More Expensive Agents

article_ideas.angle: Re-apply the OO inheritance-vs-composition argument to agent capability accumulation, using the monolithic-agent vs. coordinator-plus-sub-agents contrast as the case study.
article_ideas.audience: Software architects and agent framework authors
article_ideas.based_on: Inheritance in agents (adding endless MCPs and skills to one monolithic agent) breaks down
article_ideas.thesis: Accumulating MCP servers and skills inside one context window is inheritance, and it fails for the same reason deep inheritance hierarchies fail: coupling. Capability boundaries belong between agents, not inside one prompt, and decomposition is the only scalable path.
article_ideas.title: Composition Over Inheritance Is the Real Agent Architecture Decision

article_ideas.angle: Attack the MCP-servers-as-progress-metric mindset and describe skill registration as a context budget problem with a degradation curve.
article_ideas.based_on: Using too many agent skills can degrade agent performance.
article_ideas.thesis: MCP server count and skill count are being used as capability metrics, but declarative capability descriptions consume the same scarce context as task content and degrade performance past a threshold — capability registries need selection and routing strategies, not unconditional loading.
article_ideas.title: Integration Surface Is Not Capability

article_ideas.angle: Take the speaker's agent definition literally and unpack what becomes code versus what stays probabilistic, and what that implies for testing and provider swapping.
article_ideas.audience: Backend/platform engineers moving into agent development
article_ideas.based_on: Agents are deterministic software that harnesses the non-deterministic results produced by models in pursuit of a desired objective.
article_ideas.thesis: Treating the model as the application is the core engineering mistake; the durable, testable artifact is the deterministic harness — loop control, guardrails, hooks, and rules — that wraps bounded probabilistic calls, which is where portability, telemetry, and durability become design surfaces.
article_ideas.title: The Harness Is the Artifact

connections.relationship: Context limits are the mechanism that makes monolithic skill accumulation break down and decomposition advantageous.
Narrow scope reduces required capability, making SLMs viable where a general-purpose agent would not be.
Unconditional loading of tools and skill documentation is a candidate contributor to context bloat and rising per-task tokens.
Representing agents in the tool namespace is what enables hierarchical composition under a coordinator.

evidence_quotes.text: Agents are deterministic software that harnesses the non-deterministic results produced by models in pursuit of a desired objective.
The orchestration logic, loop control, and safety guardrails are code-driven, while the reasoning steps rely on probabilistic AI models.

core_insights.generalization: Any system embedding a probabilistic component should treat the probabilistic part as a bounded service inside deterministic code, not as the application itself.
core_insights.insight: Agents should be defined as deterministic software that harnesses non-deterministic model output — orchestration logic, loop control, and guardrails are code, while only reasoning steps are probabilistic. This makes the 'harness' a first-class engineering artifact separate from the model.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It relocates engineering effort from prompt/model tuning to the software layer (control flow, guardrails, safety) that most teams underinvest in, and gives a concrete boundary for what is and is not an 'agent'.

evidence_quotes.text: Inheritance in agents (adding endless MCPs and skills to one monolithic agent) breaks down due to diminishing returns on context.
Adding 100+ skills to Claude vs. composing specialized sub-agents for Figma, Gmail, Kayak, and Navan.

core_insights.generalization: Capability growth via accumulated context scales sublinearly; capability growth via decomposition into independently-scoped components scales better wherever context is a scarce resource.
core_insights.insight: Scaling a single agent by stacking MCP servers and skills exhibits diminishing returns on context; the composition pattern — a coordinator dispatching to narrow sub-agents (e.g., Figma, Gmail, Kayak, Navan) — is claimed to be the superior architecture. This is inheritance-vs-composition from OO design re-applied to agent capability accumulation.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It defines where capability boundaries belong: not inside one context window, but between agents. This changes how teams decompose tools, prompts, and permissions.

evidence_quotes.text: Even though raw token prices drop, the token count required per task is increasing rapidly due to context bloat and lack of efficiency.
Standard Agents tracking data showing token costs up 29% to 76% in 2026.

core_insights.generalization: When a resource gets cheaper per unit but consumption per unit of work rises faster, total cost rises; optimizations must target consumption, not unit price.
core_insights.insight: Despite falling raw token prices, per-task token cost is rising because required context per task is inflating — the speaker cites tracking data showing token costs up 29% to 76% in 2026. Cheaper tokens do not mean cheaper agents.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It inverts the common cost-model assumption that model price declines automatically improve unit economics, and makes context discipline (not model choice) the primary cost lever.

evidence_quotes.text: Domain-specific agents are far more token-efficient (80%+ savings) and make small language models (SLMs) practical.
They enforce strict capability limits, have excellent scaling characteristics, and reduce costs significantly.

core_insights.generalization: Restricting an agent's operating domain reduces context requirements, which lowers cost and simultaneously raises the viability of smaller/cheaper models for that domain.
core_insights.insight: Narrowing agent scope yields roughly 80%+ token savings, makes small language models (SLMs) practical, and enforces strict capability limits — a single mechanism that simultaneously improves cost, feasibility of cheaper models, and safety posture.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Domain scoping is presented as a coupled solution to the cost crisis and the safety/capability-control problem, rather than a product-naming choice. It also creates a viable path to SLM deployment.

evidence_quotes.text: MCP has become a de facto tool distribution mechanism for agents, but tools and documentation alone are not enough to land complex projects.
Using too many agent skills can degrade agent performance.

core_insights.generalization: Adding declarative capability descriptions consumes the same scarce context budget as task content; capability registries need their own scaling and selection strategy (e.g., retrieval/routing) rather than unconditional loading.
core_insights.insight: MCP has become a de facto tool-distribution mechanism, but tools plus markdown documentation are insufficient to complete complex projects, and overloading an agent with skills actively degrades its performance. Integration surface is not capability.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It warns against treating MCP server count or skill count as a capability metric, and identifies skills as a context-polluting resource with a degradation threshold.

evidence_quotes.text: An ideal agent stack includes a model, system prompt, tools (functions, prompts, sub-agents), hooks, agent rules, a sandbox filesystem, and code execution capabilities.
Salesforce agent talking to a Google Workspace agent and an Asset Generation agent under a coordination agent.

core_insights.generalization: Treating an agent as a uniform 'callable tool' makes recursive composition the default scaling mechanism for hierarchical agent systems.
core_insights.insight: An ideal domain-specific agent stack is enumerated as: model, system prompt, tools (functions, prompts, and sub-agents), hooks, agent rules, a sandbox filesystem, and code execution — with sub-agents as a tool type enabling recursive sub-agency under a coordinator.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It gives a concrete layer list in which sub-agents are unified with tools as a single abstraction, and where hooks/rules and a sandbox filesystem sit relative to the model — useful as a checklist for production agent design.

deep_dives.why: The composition claim is asserted with an analogy (Figma, Gmail, Kayak, Navan) but no boundary rule or benchmark. Without a measured granularity curve, teams decomposing agents are guessing, and coordination cost may silently eat the context savings.

evidence_quotes.text: Domain-specific agents are far more token-efficient (80%+ savings) and make small language models (SLMs) practical.

deep_dives.why: The savings figure and the SLM practicality claim are stated together, so teams cannot tell whether narrowing scope makes small models viable or whether a small model was doing the saving. This determines the order of operations for cost work.

evidence_quotes.text: An ideal agent stack includes a model, system prompt, tools (functions, prompts, sub-agents), hooks, agent rules, a sandbox filesystem, and code execution capabilities.

deep_dives.why: Sub-agents represented as tools make recursion the default scaling mechanism, but nesting adds overhead and makes it ambiguous where hooks, rules, and context limits apply. A depth ceiling or budget rule is needed before this becomes a production default.

Vercel's 'eve' framework as an emerging standard.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Justin Schroeder
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Domain-Specific AI Agents and Multi-Agent Orchestration
  • Purpose: To explain why domain-specific agents are the future of AI engineering, detail the agent tech stack (from models to MCP and skills), contrast inheritance with composition in agent design, and predict the rise of multi-agent orchestration by 2027. Justin Schroeder argues that the future of AI building and usage lies in domain-specific agents rather than monolithic general-purpose models. He defines agents as deterministic software harnessing non-deterministic model results, explains the challenges of current agent engineering, and introduces a stack based on composition, Model Context Protocol (MCP), agent skills, and multi-agent coordination mimicking historical engineering milestones like the Apollo program.

Topic Map

Industrial Revolution to Agential Era Analogy

  • Explanation: Drawing parallels between the industrial revolution (harnessing energy with machines) and the AI era (harnessing intelligence with agents).
  • Key claims:
    • We are in an accelerated industrial revolution for intelligence.
    • Agents are the machines of the agential era that will use intelligence.
  • Examples:
    • Harnessing energy with machines vs. harnessing intelligence with agents.
  • Terminology:
    • agential era
    • industrial revolution
  • Why it matters: Frames the current shift in AI engineering as a fundamental technological paradigm change.

Definition of an Agent

  • Explanation: Providing a precise software engineering definition for what constitutes an agent.
  • Key claims:
    • Agents are deterministic software that harnesses the non-deterministic results produced by models in pursuit of a desired objective.
  • Examples:
    • Distinction between a model, a harness, and an agent.
  • Terminology:
    • deterministic software
    • non-deterministic results
    • harness
  • Why it matters: Establishes a baseline technical definition amidst industry confusion.

The Mess of Building Agents Today

  • Explanation: Highlighting the practical difficulties engineering teams face when building custom agents.
  • Key claims:
    • Everyone is building agents, but building robust agents is hard.
    • There is no defined way to build an agent, leading to high friction in telemetry, portability, and composability.
  • Examples:
    • Real estate agencies and insurance brokers building custom agents.
    • Vercel's 'eve' framework as an emerging standard.
  • Terminology:
    • agentic loop orchestration
    • provider abstraction
    • durable execution
    • telemetry/observability
    • portability
    • composability
  • Why it matters: Explains why building agents currently feels like a nightmare for IT departments.

Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent Skills

  • Explanation: Evaluating existing integration mechanisms like MCP and Markdown-based agent skills.
  • Key claims:
    • MCP has become a de facto tool distribution mechanism for agents, but tools and documentation alone are not enough to land complex projects.
    • Using too many agent skills can degrade agent performance.
  • Examples:
    • Connecting corporate information (Zillow, American Airlines) to large general-purpose agents via MCP.
    • Markdown skill files acting as documentation.
  • Terminology:
    • Model Context Protocol (MCP)
    • agent skills
    • tool distribution
  • Why it matters: Shows the limitations of treating tools and documentation as the sole solution for agent capability.

Composition over Inheritance in Agent Design

  • Explanation: Comparing inheritance-based agent stacks with composition-based agent stacks.
  • Key claims:
    • Inheritance in agents (adding endless MCPs and skills to one monolithic agent) breaks down due to diminishing returns on context.
    • Composition (combining specialized sub-agents via a coordinator) is the superior architectural pattern.
  • Examples:
    • Adding 100+ skills to Claude vs. composing specialized sub-agents for Figma, Gmail, Kayak, and Navan.
  • Terminology:
    • inheritance
    • composition
    • context layer
    • sub-agent
  • Why it matters: Provides a clear architectural blueprint for scaling agent systems effectively.

Advantages of Domain-Specific Agents

  • Explanation: Listing the core benefits of targeting agents to very specific domains.
  • Key claims:
    • Domain-specific agents are far more token-efficient (80%+ savings) and make small language models (SLMs) practical.
    • They enforce strict capability limits, have excellent scaling characteristics, and reduce costs significantly.
  • Examples:
    • DeepSeek v4 flash vs. Fable cost comparisons.
  • Terminology:
    • token efficiency
    • small language models (SLMs)
    • scaling characteristics
    • capability limits
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates why domain-specific agents solve the token cost and safety crises of modern AI deployment.

The Ideal Agent Stack

  • Explanation: Breaking down the exact architectural layers of an ideal domain-specific agent.
  • Key claims:
    • An ideal agent stack includes a model, system prompt, tools (functions, prompts, sub-agents), hooks, agent rules, a sandbox filesystem, and code execution capabilities.
  • Examples:
    • Salesforce agent talking to a Google Workspace agent and an Asset Generation agent under a coordination agent.
  • Terminology:
    • system prompt
    • hooks
    • agent rules
    • filesystem
    • code execution
    • recursive sub-agency
  • Why it matters: Provides developers with a concrete design pattern to build production-grade agent architectures.

Key Points

Agents are deterministic software wrapped around non-deterministic models

  • Explanation: The orchestration logic, loop control, and safety guardrails are code-driven, while the reasoning steps rely on probabilistic AI models.
  • Evidence: Justin Schroeder's formal definition slide.
  • Practical implication: Developers must focus on robust software engineering around the model rather than treating the model as the entire application.

Token costs are rising, not falling, when accounting for intelligence needs

  • Explanation: Even though raw token prices drop, the token count required per task is increasing rapidly due to context bloat and lack of efficiency.
  • Evidence: Standard Agents tracking data showing token costs up 29% to 76% in 2026.
  • Practical implication: Domain-specific agents are required to restrict context windows and drastically improve token efficiency.

Composition beats inheritance in agent scaling

  • Explanation: Overloading a single agent with every tool and skill causes context degradation and high token costs. Orchestrating small, specialized agents via natural language coordination is far more effective.
  • Evidence: Analogy to software engineering principles (composition over inheritance) and multi-agent workflow diagrams.
  • Practical implication: Build modular sub-agents for specific tasks (e.g., Figma, Gmail, legal compliance) rather than one giant monolithic assistant.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

The Ideal Domain-Specific Agent Stack

  • How it works: Layers modular components from low-level execution up to high-level governance rules.
  • Components:
    • Model (LLM or SLM)
    • System Prompt (life objective)
    • Tools (functions, prompts, sub-agents)
    • Hooks (side-effects and state injection)
    • Agent Rules (turn limits and validation)
    • Sandbox Filesystem & Code Execution (native primitive)
  • When to use: When building production-ready, scalable, multi-agent enterprise systems.

Examples & Case Studies

Comparing the moon landing control room to modern AI agent systems.

  • Illustrates: Multi-agent orchestration and division of labor.
  • Lesson: Just as Apollo 11 succeeded through specialized teams of experts with specific tools and narrow communication channels, AI systems succeed through coordinated domain-specific sub-agents.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Stop building monolithic general-purpose agents.
    • Adopt composition over inheritance when designing agent capabilities.
    • Incorporate sandbox filesystems and code execution as core agent primitives.
  • Strategic:
    • Prepare for the rise of multi-agent orchestration by 2027.
    • Leverage small language models (SLMs) with domain-specific agents to achieve 80%+ token efficiency and dramatic cost reductions.
    • Focus engineering efforts on agent telemetry, durability, and loop orchestration.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How do we standardize agent portability across different runtime environments?
    • What are the best frameworks for managing recursive sub-agent turn coordination?
    • How can telemetry and observability be effectively implemented at scale for multi-agent loops?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Token costs per intelligence point are up 29% to 76% in 2026 (market statistic)
  • Domain-specific agents achieve over 80% token efficiency compared to general agents (technical benchmark claim)

Notable Quotes

"Agents are deterministic software that harnesses the non-deterministic results produced by models in pursuit of a desired objective." (at 3:45) "Composition over inheritance." (at 20:56) "We didn't land a man on the moon by giving one guy a ton of tools." (at 15:00)

Compressed Summary

  • Domain-specific agents solve the token cost and context bloat crisis of modern AI.
  • Composition over inheritance: modular sub-agents outperform monolithic general assistants.
  • The ideal agent stack features sandboxed filesystems, code execution, hooks, and natural language multi-agent coordination.
  • 2027 will be the year of multi-agent orchestration.
  • Keywords: domain-specific agents, multi-agent orchestration, model context protocol, agent stack, token efficiency
  • Core insight: Monolithic general-purpose agents fail at scale due to token costs and context degradation; the future belongs to composed ecosystems of domain-specific sub-agents communicating via natural language.

  - Distinction between a model, a harness, and an agent.
- **Terminology**:
  - deterministic software
  - non-deterministic results
  - harness
- **Why it matters**: Establishes a baseline technical definition amidst industry confusion.
### The Mess of Building Agents Today
- **Explanation**: Highlighting the practical difficulties engineering teams face when building custom agents.
- **Key claims**:
  - Everyone is building agents, but building robust agents is hard.
  - There is no defined way to build an agent, leading to high friction in telemetry, portability, and composability.
- **Examples**:
  - Real estate agencies and insurance brokers building custom agents.
  - Vercel's 'eve' framework as an emerging standard.
- **Terminology**:
  - agentic loop orchestration
  - provider abstraction
  - durable execution
  - telemetry/observability
  - portability
  - composability
- **Why it matters**: Explains why building agents currently feels like a nightmare for IT departments.
### Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent Skills
- **Explanation**: Evaluating existing integration mechanisms like MCP and Markdown-based agent skills.
- **Key claims**:
  - MCP has become a de facto tool distribution mechanism for agents, but tools and documentation alone are not enough to land complex projects.
  - Using too many agent skills can degrade agent performance.
- **Examples**:
  - Connecting corporate information (Zillow, American Airlines) to large general-purpose agents via MCP.
  - Markdown skill files acting as documentation.
- **Terminology**:
  - Model Context Protocol (MCP)
  - agent skills
  - tool distribution
- **Why it matters**: Shows the limitations of treating tools and documentation as the sole solution for agent capability.
### Composition over Inheritance in Agent Design
- **Explanation**: Comparing inheritance-based agent stacks with composition-based agent stacks.
- **Key claims**:
  - Inheritance in agents (adding endless MCPs and skills to one monolithic agent) breaks down due to diminishing returns on context.
  - Composition (combining specialized sub-agents via a coordinator) is the superior architectural pattern.
- **Examples**:
  - Adding 100+ skills to Claude vs. composing specialized sub-agents for Figma, Gmail, Kayak, and Navan.
- **Terminology**:
  - inheritance
  - composition
  - context layer
  - sub-agent
- **Why it matters**: Provides a clear architectural blueprint for scaling agent systems effectively.
### Advantages of Domain-Specific Agents
- **Explanation**: Listing the core benefits of targeting agents to very specific domains.
- **Key claims**:
  - Domain-specific agents are far more token-efficient (80%+ savings) and make small language models (SLMs) practical.
  - They enforce strict capability limits, have excellent scaling characteristics, and reduce costs significantly.
- **Examples**:
  - DeepSeek v4 flash vs. Fable cost comparisons.
- **Terminology**:
  - token efficiency
  - small language models (SLMs)
  - scaling characteristics
  - capability limits
- **Why it matters**: Demonstrates why domain-specific agents solve the token cost and safety crises of modern AI deployment.
### The Ideal Agent Stack
- **Explanation**: Breaking down the exact architectural layers of an ideal domain-specific agent.
- **Key claims**:
  - An ideal agent stack includes a model, system prompt, tools (functions, prompts, sub-agents), hooks, agent rules, a sandbox filesystem, and code execution capabilities.
- **Examples**:
  - Salesforce agent talking to a Google Workspace agent and an Asset Generation agent under a coordination agent.
- **Terminology**:
  - system prompt
  - hooks
  - agent rules
  - filesystem
  - code execution
  - recursive sub-agency
- **Why it matters**: Provides developers with a concrete design pattern to build production-grade agent architectures.
## Key Points
### Agents are deterministic software wrapped around non-deterministic models
- **Explanation**: The orchestration logic, loop control, and safety guardrails are code-driven, while the reasoning steps rely on probabilistic AI models.
- **Evidence**: Justin Schroeder's formal definition slide.
- **Practical implication**: Developers must focus on robust software engineering around the model rather than treating the model as the entire application.
### Token costs are rising, not falling, when accounting for intelligence needs
- **Explanation**: Even though raw token prices drop, the token count required per task is increasing rapidly due to context bloat and lack of efficiency.
- **Evidence**: Standard Agents tracking data showing token costs up 29% to 76% in 2026.
- **Practical implication**: Domain-specific agents are required to restrict context windows and drastically improve token efficiency.
### Composition beats inheritance in agent scaling
- **Explanation**: Overloading a single agent with every tool and skill causes context degradation and high token costs. Orchestrating small, specialized agents via natural language coordination is far more effective.
- **Evidence**: Analogy to software engineering principles (composition over inheritance) and multi-agent workflow diagrams.
- **Practical implication**: Build modular sub-agents for specific tasks (e.g., Figma, Gmail, legal compliance) rather than one giant monolithic assistant.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### The Ideal Domain-Specific Agent Stack
- **How it works**: Layers modular components from low-level execution up to high-level governance rules.
- **Components**:
  - Model (LLM or SLM)
  - System Prompt (life objective)
  - Tools (functions, prompts, sub-agents)
  - Hooks (side-effects and state injection)
  - Agent Rules (turn limits and validation)
  - Sandbox Filesystem & Code Execution (native primitive)
- **When to use**: When building production-ready, scalable, multi-agent enterprise systems.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Comparing the moon landing control room to modern AI agent systems.
- **Illustrates**: Multi-agent orchestration and division of labor.
- **Lesson**: Just as Apollo 11 succeeded through specialized teams of experts with specific tools and narrow communication channels, AI systems succeed through coordinated domain-specific sub-agents.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Stop building monolithic general-purpose agents.
  - Adopt composition over inheritance when designing agent capabilities.
  - Incorporate sandbox filesystems and code execution as core agent primitives.
- **Strategic**:
  - Prepare for the rise of multi-agent orchestration by 2027.
  - Leverage small language models (SLMs) with domain-specific agents to achieve 80%+ token efficiency and dramatic cost reductions.
  - Focus engineering efforts on agent telemetry, durability, and loop orchestration.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How do we standardize agent portability across different runtime environments?
  - What are the best frameworks for managing recursive sub-agent turn coordination?
  - How can telemetry and observability be effectively implemented at scale for multi-agent loops?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Token costs per intelligence point are up 29% to 76% in 2026 (market statistic)
- Domain-specific agents achieve over 80% token efficiency compared to general agents (technical benchmark claim)
## Notable Quotes
> "Agents are deterministic software that harnesses the non-deterministic results produced by models in pursuit of a desired objective." (at 3:45)
> "Composition over inheritance." (at 20:56)
> "We didn't land a man on the moon by giving one guy a ton of tools." (at 15:00)
## Compressed Summary
- Domain-specific agents solve the token cost and context bloat crisis of modern AI.
- Composition over inheritance: modular sub-agents outperform monolithic general assistants.
- The ideal agent stack features sandboxed filesystems, code execution, hooks, and natural language multi-agent coordination.
- 2027 will be the year of multi-agent orchestration.
- **Keywords**: domain-specific agents, multi-agent orchestration, model context protocol, agent stack, token efficiency
- **Core insight**: Monolithic general-purpose agents fail at scale due to token costs and context degradation; the future belongs to composed ecosystems of domain-specific sub-agents communicating via natural language.
